endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Integrate tools designed to analyze content provenance and detect data anomalies, verify the authenticity of digital signatures, and identify patterns associated with misinformation or manipulation.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: These guidelines should include requiring the disclosure that AI was used in research methods and data collection, requiring the exclusion of AI systems as authors, and should outline the responsibility of the authors to validate the veracity of any referenced content generated by AI.

evidence.title: CARE: A Conformal Safety Layer for Medical Summarization
evidence.outcome: Hallucination and omission flagging
evidence.effect: CARE preserved formal guarantees while surfacing up to 5$\times$ fewer sentences than alternative calibrated baselines.
evidence.quote: By jointly calibrating over the full $(τ,γ)$ threshold space, CARE preserves formal guarantees while surfacing up to 5$\times$ fewer sentences than alternative calibrated baselines.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Colonoscopy Preparation Assistance: Correctness and Diversity in Synthetic Dialogues
evidence.outcome: error rates after automated filtering
evidence.effect: Reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.
evidence.quote: Applying an automated safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.
evidence.sample_unit: synthetic patient-AI Coach dialogues (250 per model x 5 models)

evidence.title: Assessing Llm Hallucinations And The Reliability Of Using LLms For Automated Hallucination Detection
evidence.outcome: automated hallucination detection agreement
evidence.effect: LLJs achieved up to 65.7% agreement on presence and 64.7% on subcategorization.
evidence.quote: Across automated hallucination detection, LLJs demonstrate reasonable alignment with human raters, achieving up to 65.7% agreement on hallucination presence and 64.7% agreement on hallucination subcategorization.

evidence.title: The need for guardrails with large language models in pharmacovigilance and other medical safety critical settings
evidence.outcome: hallucinated drug-name flagging
evidence.effect: In 20 randomly selected cases, MISMATCH correctly identified all spontaneously hallucinated drug names; dictionary incompleteness and drug spelling issues still caused misses.
evidence.quote: As can be seen in Fig. 4 , all instances of the never event, “spontaneously hallucinated drug names”, were correctly identified by the MISMATCH guardrail.
evidence.sample_unit: Japanese individual case safety reports (ICSRs) translated to English and reviewed by experts

evidence.title: Retrieval-Augmented Guardrails for AI-Drafted Patient-Portal Messages: Error Taxonomy Construction and Large-Scale Evaluation
evidence.venue: Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing. Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing
evidence.outcome: Error checking agreement and F1
evidence.effect: Concordance = 50% vs. 33%; F1 = 0.500 vs. 0.256 for context-enhanced labels vs. baseline.
evidence.quote: Human validation on 100 messages demonstrated superior agreement (concordance = 50% vs. 33%) and performance (F1 = 0.500 vs. 0.256) of context-enhanced labels vs. baseline, supporting the use of our RAEC pipeline as AI guardrails for patient messaging.

evidence.title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
evidence.outcome: LLM-as-judge hallucination detection
evidence.effect: Kendall W for hallucination detection was 0.37–0.55 across models/prompt detail; authors advised against LLM-as-Judges for semantic hallucinations.
evidence.quote: In general, all models showed rather low consistency with experts, which indicates the weak ability of LLM to detect semantic hallucinations in medical texts.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

evidence.title: Fact-Checking Large Language Model Responses to a Health Care Prompt: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy and speed of LLM fact-checking of generated medical claims versus expert pharmacists
evidence.effect: On 20 claims, GPT-4o agreed 100% and OpenBioLLM-70B 95% with experts. For the acne response both agreed 86%, but the LLM consistency check missed an internal inconsistency about stopping isotretinoin. GPT-4o took 42 seconds versus 18 minutes for experts.
evidence.quote: This inconsistency was not detected by the consistency check ( Textbox 3 ).
evidence.sample_unit: clinical claims (plus one acne scenario with 16 expert-identified claims)

evidence.title: Improving Reliability and Explainability of Medical Question Answering Through Atomic Fact-Checking in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models: Creation and Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Answer quality on AMEGA benchmark with atomic fact-checking versus RAG alone
evidence.effect: Significant improvement for all LLMs tested (P<.001 for 13/16 models, P<.01 for 2/16, P<.05 for 1/16); human-rated overall answer improvement up to 50% on tumor board cases.
evidence.quote: The AMEGA auto-evaluation analysis revealed a significant improvement in answer quality by applying our fact-checking algorithm in contrast to RAG only for all LLMs tested ( P <.001 for 13/16 models, P <.01 for 2/16 models, and P <.05 for 1/16 models; Figure 3 ; see Table S6 in Multimedia Appendix 1 ).

evidence.title: Blending Human and LLM Expertise to Detect Hallucinations and Omissions in Mental Health Chatbot Responses
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of automated hallucination and omission detection in mental health chatbot responses, LLM judges versus expert-informed features
evidence.effect: LLM judges reached only 52% accuracy, with some near-zero recall. Expert-informed feature models reached 0.717 F1 (custom dataset) and 0.849 F1 (public benchmark) for hallucinations, and 0.59-0.64 F1 for omissions.
evidence.quote: We show that leading LLM judges achieve only 52% accuracy on mental health counseling data, with some hallucination detection approaches exhibiting near-zero recall.

evidence.title: CuraView: A Multi-Agent Framework for Medical Hallucination Detection with GraphRAG-Enhanced Knowledge Verification
evidence.outcome: Sentence-level detection of faithfulness hallucinations in LLM-generated discharge summaries (F1, recall, precision)
evidence.effect: Fine-tuned Qwen3-14B detector: E4 F1 0.831 (90.9% recall, 76.5% precision); E3+E4 F1 0.823, a 50.0% relative improvement over base model and better than RAGTruth-style and QAGS-style baselines.
evidence.quote: Our fine-tuned Qwen3-14B detection model achieves an F1 of 0.831 on the safety-critical E4 metric (90.9% recall, 76.5% precision) and an F1 of 0.823 on E3+E4, representing a 50.0% relative improvement over the base model and outperforming RAGTruth-style and QAGS-style baselines.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (held-out test set from 250 patients in the Discharge-Me benchmark)

evidence.title: MedFabric: Gold Evidence Hides the Difficulty of Word-Level Medical Fabrication Detection
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of fabrication detectors (macro F1) across evidence conditions, including expert clinicians
evidence.effect: Expert clinicians reached 53.3% macro F1 and no detector family cleared about 60% without gold evidence. A strong LLM scored 91% with gold evidence and 35% with wrong evidence.
evidence.quote: On MedFabric the task is unsolved: expert clinicians reach only 53.3% macro F1 and no detector family clears about 60% without gold evidence.

evidence.title: ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents
evidence.outcome: Block F1 and source accuracy of automated claim-level verifier on held-out medical agent traces
evidence.effect: Block F1 0.802 and source accuracy 0.858 over 260 source-eligible claims on the 40-trace held-out split; outperformed source-blind baselines. Harder multi-source benchmark: block F1 0.846.
evidence.quote: On the 40-trace held-out split, ProvenanceGuard achieves block F1 0.802 and source accuracy 0.858 over 260 source-eligible claims, outperforming source-blind baselines that do not emit claim-to-source IDs.

evidence.title: Expert-level validation of AI-generated medical text with scalable language models
evidence.outcome: Automated LM validator detection of factual inconsistencies in generated medical outputs versus physician review
evidence.effect: Average F1 rose from 66% to 83% after MedVAL fine-tuning (p < 0.001); safety classification up to 86%.
evidence.quote: MedVAL fine-tuning significantly improves (p < 0.001) alignment with physicians on both seen and unseen tasks, increasing average F1 scores from 66% to 83%, with per-sample safety classification scores up to 86%.

evidence.title: Architectural Hallucination Mitigation in Multi-Agent Document Intelligence: Domain-Isolated RAG and Dual-Channel Claim Verification
evidence.outcome: Delivered hallucination and claim precision
evidence.effect: C2 reduces delivered hallucination from 10.0% to 0.29% at 97.1% claim precision.
evidence.quote: Calibrated on 1,240 documents (8,431 claims), C2 reduces delivered hallucination from 10.0% to 0.29% at 97.1% claim precision.

evidence.title: VaaS is a Multi-Layer Hallucination Reduction Pipeline for AI-Assisted Science: Production Validation and Prospective Benchmarking
evidence.outcome: Clinical hallucination benchmark performance
evidence.effect: VaaS F1 = 0.9853 on MedHallu hard tier versus published GPT-4o baseline F1 = 0.811.
evidence.quote: We validated the pipeline using three complementary benchmarks: (1) VaaS-RIKER2, a 640-run prospective ablation study (4 conditions × 4 temperatures × 40 genes) plus 117 open-weight model runs on dedicated GPU hardware — unguided LLM output produced 95.9% Type II hallucination (wrong-topic citations that exist as real papers but carry a correct claim context yet do not support the cited claim); the full VaaS protocol achieved 0.0% Type I and 6.5% Type II, a  > 14-fold reduction; live PMID verification alone (C3) eliminated both error types entirely (0.0%/0.0%); (2) an independent L3 citation audit of Wave 3 (179 PMIDs, 99.4% valid, 0 Type I errors); and (3) the MedHallu clinical hallucination benchmark, on which the VaaS protocol achieved F1 = 0.9853 on the hard tier (cases where all benchmark ensemble models were fooled), compared to the published GPT-4o baseline of F1 = 0.811 (Pandit et al., 2025).
evidence.sample_unit: benchmark runs (4 conditions x 4 temperatures x 40 genes)

evidence.title: Human–Agent Joint Diagnosis with ValidLLP4LLM: A Labeled Logic Framework for Validating LLM Reasoning
evidence.outcome: Hallucination detection performance of LLP-based validation versus classical symbolic validators on benchmark datasets
evidence.effect: LLP-based validation improved over classical symbolic validators, especially with discourse modeling. Performance on the challenging clinical narrative dataset was weaker, showing difficulty with implicit, ambiguous language. No numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Experiments on benchmark hallucination-detection datasets show that LLP-based validation improves over classical symbolic validators, especially when combined with discourse modeling, while results on a challenging clinical narrative dataset highlight the difficulty of verifying implicit, ambiguous, and underspecified patient language.

evidence.title: Citation Hallucination Determines Success: An Empirical Comparison of Six Medical AI Research Systems
evidence.outcome: Citation integrity and weighted total score before and after adding multi-agent citation verification and repair pipeline
evidence.effect: Citation integrity score rose from 40.0 to 90.9; weighted total rose from 68.9 to 81.8 for the best-performing system.
evidence.quote: Adding a multi-agent citation verification and repair pipeline to the best-performing system improved its citation integrity score from 40.0 to 90.9 and raised the weighted total from 68.9 to 81.8.
evidence.sample_unit: AI research systems (evaluated on 3 NHANES clinical epidemiology tasks)

evidence.title: ChainTrust-LLM: Secure and Auditable Hallucination Mitigation in Medical LLMs Using Blockchain and Expert Feedback
evidence.outcome: hallucination rates and trust calibration
evidence.effect: Hallucination rates reduced by up to 64.8%; trust calibration accuracy improved by 23.4%.
evidence.quote: Extensive evaluation using GPT-4, MedPaLM, and Claude across 300 curated medical prompts demonstrates that ChainTrust-LLM reduces hallucination rates by up to 64.8%, improves trust calibration accuracy by 23.4%, and enhances inter-rater agreement (Fleiss’ k) from 0.65 to 0.87.

evidence.title: Citation reliability of frontier large language models in medical writing and its automated verification
evidence.outcome: automated verification sensitivity and specificity for problematic references
evidence.effect: CoVe detected 60 of 62 problematic references with 96.8% sensitivity and 98.6% specificity, including every misattribution and fabrication
evidence.quote: Against an expert-adjudicated set of 270 references, an LLM-based Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) detected 60 of 62 problematic references (sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 98.6%), including every misattribution and fabrication.

evidence.title: Medical large language models are vulnerable to data-poisoning attacks
evidence.outcome: Share of harmful LLM output captured by knowledge-graph screening
evidence.effect: Knowledge-graph screening captured 91.9% of harmful content (F1 = 85.7%).
evidence.quote: Using biomedical knowledge graphs to screen medical LLM outputs, we propose a harm mitigation strategy that captures 91.9% of harmful content (F1 = 85.7%).
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs trained (1.3B and 4B parameter) with simulated poisoning of The Pile

evidence.title: Benchmarking large language model-based agent systems for clinical decision tasks
evidence.outcome: Share of hallucinations filtered by in-agent safeguards
evidence.effect: 89.9% of hallucinations were filtered by in-agent safeguards, but hallucinations remained prevalent.
evidence.quote: Although 89.9% of hallucinations were filtered by in-agent safeguards, hallucinations remained prevalent.

evidence.title: Enhancing the quality and trustworthiness of large language model-generated summaries of clinical oncology literature
evidence.outcome: Agreement of multi-LLM panel fact-checking with human experts in detecting unfaithful summary facts
evidence.effect: LLM panel vs human panel kappa 0.67 (95% CI 0.61-0.73) at 4/5 LLM agreement; verification scores fell as fact modifications became more severe, showing sensitive error detection.
evidence.quote: The maximum score for agreement between LLM panel and human experts panel (Cohen’s kappa 0.67 [95% CI, 0.61–0.73]) was observed when a panel of 4 LLMs agreed that the fact was faithful to the original title/abstract, suggesting that acceptance of facts by 4/5 LLMs maximizes agreement with the human panel ( Figure S1A ).

evidence.title: Real-time hallucination detection and intervention in medical LLMs via calibrated hidden-state probes
evidence.outcome: Hallucination detection and flagging of generated medical answers under false-positive-rate caps
evidence.effect: EDR@5 up to 0.390 (PubMedQA) and 0.352 (MedHallu) at strict cap γ≤0.10, rising to 0.587 with 29%-59% hallucination reduction at monitoring cap γ≤0.20.
evidence.quote: The trigger fires roughly 10-35 tokens before error onset, whereas a post-hoc check has zero lead time by construction.

evidence.title: Swin-Qwen3: a three-stage vision-language framework for automated radiology report generation with multi-agent verification
evidence.outcome: Hallucination correction by the verifier stage and overall hallucination rate and factuality across one-, two-, three-stage variants
evidence.effect: Verifier corrected 85.6% of identified hallucinations, but the hallucination rate stayed 0.6116 (three-stage) vs 0.6109 (one/two-stage) and factuality was 0.843 vs 0.845.
evidence.quote: However, the clinical verifier demonstrated substantial effectiveness, correcting 85.6% of identified hallucinations.

evidence.title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
evidence.outcome: Whether LLMs flag or block health misinformation outputs
evidence.effect: Three of the evaluated LLMs generated 113 unique cancer disinformation blogs (over 40,000 words) with fake references and testimonials; refusal rate 5% (7 of 150).
evidence.quote: The refusal rate across the evaluation timepoints for these LLMs was only 5% (7 of 150), and as prompted the LLM generated blogs incorporated attention grabbing titles, authentic looking (fake or fictional) references, fabricated testimonials from patients and clinicians, and they targeted diverse demographic groups.

evidence.title: Large Language Models: Pioneering New Educational Frontiers in Childhood Myopia
evidence.outcome: Misinformation in LLM-generated patient education materials on Likert scale
evidence.effect: All 120 responses scored 1 (no misinformation) across the three LLMs.
evidence.quote: All 120 responses received a score of 1 on the Likert misinformation scale, indicating that these three LLMs did not produce any misinformation across the 120 newly generated PEMs.

evidence.title: How Accurate Is AI? A Critical Evaluation of Commonly Used Large Language Models in Responding to Patient Concerns About Incidental Kidney Tumors
evidence.outcome: Rate of misleading or incomplete LLM responses rated by urologists
evidence.effect: 14% of responses flagged as potentially misleading or incomplete; Gemini accuracy 4.3, hallucination score 4.6.
evidence.quote: Overall, 14% of responses were flagged as potentially misleading or incomplete.

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT's ability to simplify scientific abstracts for clinicians and the public
evidence.outcome: Hallucination presence in ChatGPT-generated abstract summaries rated by reviewers
evidence.effect: Hallucination presence scored below 7 out of 10; hallucination scores varied by study type, with case reports lowest.
evidence.quote: Despite its strengths, ChatGPT showed limitations in "Hallucination presence" and "Technical terms usage," scoring below 7 out of 10.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Large Language Models in Addressing Patient Queries Regarding Maxillomandibular Fixation for Maxillofacial Fractures
evidence.venue: Journal of oral and maxillofacial surgery : official journal of the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons
evidence.outcome: Hallucination (fabricated content) rate in LLM answers to MMF questions
evidence.effect: DOT-1 hallucination rate 5.2% vs DOT-2 10.1% and PM 9.4% (P = .013); accuracy ranged from 79.6% to 88.5%.
evidence.quote: It also had a statistically significantly lower hallucination rate (5.2%) compared with DOT-2 (10.1%) and PM (9.4%) (P = .013).

evidence.title: Freely accessible large language models for parent education in pediatric immune thrombocytopenia: an expert-rated cross-sectional study of safety, readability, and guideline concordance
evidence.outcome: Unsafe-content and hallucination events in LLM responses to parent ITP questions
evidence.effect: Two response-level unsafe-content/hallucination events, both in Gemini 3 Flash responses (2/40, 5.0%; exact 95% CI, 0.6%-16.9%); involved overgeneralized autoimmune-testing advice and unsupported MMR vaccination counseling.
evidence.quote: Two response-level unsafe-content and hallucination events were detected, both in Gemini 3 Flash responses (2/40, 5.0%; exact 95% CI, 0.6%-16.9%).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (40 questions x 3 models), rated by 3 reviewers (360 assessments)

evidence.title: Using Large Language Models to Generate Retina Patient Education Material: A Comparative Analysis With American Society of Retina Specialists Patient Brochures
evidence.outcome: Misinformation in generated materials
evidence.effect: Misinformation was graded using a 5-point Likert scale; no significant differences were observed for misinformation.
evidence.quote: No significant differences were observed for actionability or misinformation.
evidence.sample_unit: patient education materials (3 retinal conditions x 3 LLMs x 2 prompts, plus ASRS brochures)

evidence.title: ChatGPT Responses to Frequently Asked Questions on Ménière's Disease: A Comparison to Clinical Practice Guideline Answers
evidence.outcome: Presence of misleading information in ChatGPT responses to Ménière's disease FAQs
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-3.5 misleading in 5 of 16 responses and ChatGPT-4.0 in 3 of 16 (31.3% vs 18.75%, P = .6851).
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-3.5 was misleading in 5 responses whereas ChatGPT-4.0 was misleading in 3 (31.3% vs 18.75%, P = .6851).

evidence.title: Mapping the susceptibility of large language models to medical misinformation across clinical notes and social media: a cross-sectional benchmarking analysis
evidence.outcome: Model detection of misinformation and logical-fallacy rhetoric in prompts
evidence.effect: LLMs accepted fabricated claims in 31.7% of base prompts. GPT models were least susceptible and most accurate at fallacy detection; other models such as Gemma-3-4B-it were susceptible in 63.6% (5,023/7,900).
evidence.quote: Performance varied by model: GPT models were the least susceptible and most accurate at fallacy detection, whereas others, such as Gemma-3-4B-it, showed 63·6% (5023 of 7900) susceptibility.
evidence.sample_unit: base prompts (of >3.4 million total prompts across 20 LLMs)

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-four studies test automated fact-checking or hallucination detection on generative AI outputs, but all were offline or benchmark evaluations, and none measured whether flagging kept inaccurate content from reaching patients or staff. Purpose-built detectors reported F1 values of 0.80 to 0.98 on benchmarks, while general LLM-as-judge approaches agreed with experts roughly half to two thirds of the time.

perspectives.view: All 24 studies use level 4 or 5 designs run offline or on benchmarks, so they apply only indirectly to real dissemination. Results are inconsistent across methods. Fine-tuned detectors scored higher than LLM judges, and no study reports patient or staff outcomes. Certainty that the practice prevents misinformation from spreading is very low.

Detection reduced errors but did not remove them. Automated filtering lowered error rates without eliminating harmful responses. In-agent safeguards filtered 89.9% of hallucinations, yet hallucinations remained prevalent. A verifier corrected 85.6% of identified hallucinations while the hallucination rate stayed near 0.61. These results suggest flagging may serve as one layer that still requires human review.

Checker performance depended on the evidence it could consult. A strong LLM scored 91% with gold evidence and 35% with wrong evidence, and expert clinicians reached 53.3% macro F1. Early detection rates were 0.352 to 0.390 under strict false-positive caps. CARE surfaced up to 5 times fewer sentences for review, which may reduce reviewer burden.

In one small study, GPT-4o checked claims in 42 seconds versus 18 minutes for expert pharmacists and agreed on all 20 claims. It missed an internal inconsistency in a longer response. Atomic fact-checking improved answer quality across 16 models. No study reports implementation cost, staffing needs, or tool maintenance.

Two studies used non-English source material, Japanese safety reports and Russian EHR summaries. The drug-name checker caught every hallucinated name in 20 cases but missed errors caused by dictionary gaps and spelling. LLM judges on the Russian summaries showed Kendall W of 0.37 to 0.55. No study tested patient-facing content for low-literacy readers.

NIST AI 600-1 advises integrating tools that identify patterns of misinformation. The Principles for augmented intelligence guidance assigns authors responsibility for validating the veracity of AI-generated referenced content. Neither source sets performance thresholds, and the supplied studies do not establish a validated benchmark against which an organization could judge a documented tool.

Every evaluation stopped before content reached patients. In simulated patient-coach dialogues, harmful responses remained after filtering. On 1,500 patient messages, the best error-checking F1 was 0.500. These findings suggest patients may still receive inaccurate content even when checking tools are in place.

commentary.research_gap: No study deployed a fact-checking tool in a live workflow and compared how much inaccurate content reached patients or staff with and without flagging. Prospective comparisons in patient-facing channels would address this gap if they reported false-positive burden on reviewers, missed harmful content, and performance on non-English and plain-language materials.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests used non-English source content. One caught all hallucinated drug names in 20 Japanese case safety reports but missed errors from dictionary gaps and spelling, and the other found low agreement among LLM judges on Russian EHR summaries. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence cannot show whether these tools catch misinformation in materials written for those patients.
